title: Pressure
examples: Teacher, what makes something feel like it has more pressure?
Can you explain how air pressure works around us?
If I push something hard, does it matter how big my push area is?

explain.say: Today we will learn about pressure in physics. Pressure is a measure of force spread over an area. We calculate it using the formula P equals F divided by A.
A small force over a small area makes high pressure. For example, a sharp nail has a very small area at the point. This creates high pressure.
Knives cut easily because they have a very sharp edge. This means the force is concentrated on a tiny area. This creates enough pressure to cut things.
Air pressure pushes on everything around us all the time. Even when it seems calm, the air is pushing down on you. This is why we feel it all the time.
Water pressure increases as you go deeper underwater. This is because the weight of the water above you pushes down. Deeper means more pressure.
Think about walking on snow with snowshoes. The snowshoes spread your weight over a much larger area. This lowers the pressure so you do not sink.

faq.q: Why does a sharp object create so much pressure?
faq.a: A sharp object concentrates the force onto a very small area. This makes the pressure very high, allowing it to cut materials easily. You could also ask: Why are needles so effective at piercing things? Or: How is a sharp edge related to pressure?
asks: Why is a knife so good at cutting?
What makes a point so strong?

faq.q: Does the depth of water affect the pressure?
faq.a: Yes, the deeper you go in water, the greater the pressure becomes. This is because the weight of the water column above you increases the force. You might also ask: Why do deep-sea divers need special gear? Or: How does water pressure change with depth?
asks: Does water get harder the deeper I go?
What makes deep water push so hard?

faq.q: Is air pressure always pushing on us?
faq.a: Yes, air pressure surrounds us constantly, pushing equally from all directions. This pressure is what keeps our bodies supported in the air. Other ways to ask: What is the pressure of the air around me? Or: Does the air push on me all the time?
asks: Do I live in a vacuum?
What is the force of the air?

faq.q: How do snowshoes help us walk on snow?
faq.a: Snowshoes work by increasing the area over which your weight is spread. By increasing the area, you decrease the pressure, preventing you from sinking into the snow. You could also ask: Why do people use snowshoes? Or: How does area affect snow walking?
asks: Why don't people sink in deep snow?
What is the relationship between area and snow?

faq.q: Is pressure only about pushing down?
faq.a: No, pressure is force over area, and force can be applied in any direction. The pressure from air or water acts equally in all directions. You might also ask: Can pressure come from the sides? Or: Does pressure always go down?
asks: Does pressure have to be vertical?

facts: Pressure is calculated by dividing force by area (P = F / A).
A smaller area results in higher pressure for the same force.
Water pressure increases with depth because more water weight is above.
Air pressure surrounds us constantly, even when we do not notice it.

quiz.say: A student pushes with a constant force on a large wooden block and then on a small nail head. Which object exerts the highest pressure?

options.show: It depends on the force used
options.say: It depends on the force used

options.show: The pressure is always the same
options.say: The pressure is always the same

quiz.why: The nail head has a much smaller area, concentrating the force and creating higher pressure.

wrong.0: This is tempting because the force is the same, but the area is much bigger, which lowers the pressure.
wrong.1: This confuses the relationship; while force matters, the area is the key factor when comparing the same force.
wrong.2: This ignores the fundamental formula that pressure changes when area changes.

quiz.say: If you double the force applied to a fixed area, what happens to the pressure?
quiz.why: Since pressure is directly proportional to force, doubling the force doubles the resulting pressure.

wrong.1: This incorrectly assumes that changing force has no effect on pressure.
wrong.2: This confuses the relationship with area; increasing force must increase pressure.
wrong.3: This confuses the relationship with area, perhaps thinking about a squared relationship.

quiz.say: When comparing the pressure exerted by deep water versus shallow water, which statement is correct?

options.show: Pressure is only affected by the object's size
options.say: Pressure is only affected by the object's size

options.show: The pressure is the same at all depths
options.say: The pressure is the same at all depths

quiz.why: The deeper the water, the more water weight is pressing down, which increases the pressure.

wrong.0: This wrongly suggests that the object itself, not the surrounding fluid, determines the pressure.
wrong.2: This is incorrect because the weight of the water column is the determining factor for pressure.
wrong.3: This ignores the fact that the weight of the water above changes with depth.
